detailed_findings.finding: The reduction from Q(q) in Q[q] to divisibility D | N in Q[q], and the transfer of divisibility between Q and C, is mathematically sound.

The root-multiplicity analysis is correct: 1-q^m has a simple root at alpha exactly when alpha is a root of unity with order dividing m, so the multiplicities in N and D are exactly the counting functions mu_n(A,d) and mu_n(B,d).

reason: The proof gives a complete equivalence. It correctly reduces polynomiality of N/D to divisibility D | N in Q[q], justifies that divisibility over Q is equivalent to divisibility over C, and then characterizes divisibility over C by comparing root multiplicities at every complex number. The multiplicity of a factor 1-q^m at a complex number alpha is correctly shown to be 1 exactly when alpha is a root of unity whose order divides m, and 0 otherwise; summing these multiplicities over the product gives precisely mu_n(B,d) and mu_n(A,d). Since primitive n-th roots exist for every positive integer n, this yields the claimed iff criterion. No undeclared or forbidden dependencies are used.
